commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

The paper you're looking for is arXiv 2403.16952, by Jiasheng Ye, Peiju Liu, Tianxiang Sun, Jun Zhan, Yunhua Zhou, and Xipeng Qiu (Fudan University and Shanghai AI Laboratory). It was published at ICLR 2025.

**Core idea:** The authors argue that the mixing proportions of pretraining domains affect model quality, and that existing methods tune those proportions by heuristics. They report that performance can be predicted from the mixture proportions using functional forms, which they call data mixing laws. Fitting such functions on sample mixtures unveils model performance on unseen mixtures before actual runs, thus guiding the selection of an ideal data mixture.

**Scaling extension:** The authors also combine data mixing laws with scaling laws for training steps and model size. This lets them predict the performance of large models trained on massive data under various mixtures with only small-scale training.

**Results:** Their method effectively optimizes the training mixture of a 1B model trained for 100B tokens in RedPajama, reaching a performance comparable to the one trained for 48% more steps on the default mixture. They also note that the approach accurately predicts the critical mixture proportion that avoids catastrophic forgetting in continual training.

**Where to find it:** The arXiv HTML version is at arxiv.org/html/2403.16952v1, and the authors' code and data are on GitHub under yegcjs/mixinglaws. The ICLR 2025 BibTeX entry is listed at mlanthology.org.

The paper is "To Code, or Not To Code? Exploring Impact of Code in Pre-training" by Viraat Aryabumi and nine co-authors at Cohere For AI and Cohere. It was posted to arXiv (2408.10914) in August 2024 and later appeared at ICLR 2025.

**Research question:** The authors asked how code in pre-training data affects downstream tasks beyond code generation. Including code in the pre-training data mixture, even for models not specifically designed for code, has become a common practice in LLM pre-training. Yet there is only limited work analyzing the precise impact of code on non-code tasks.

**Method:** The team ran extensive ablations and evaluated across natural language reasoning tasks, world knowledge tasks, code benchmarks, and LLM-as-a-judge win-rates, for models ranging from 470M to 2.8B parameters.

**Key findings:**
- Compared with text-only pre-training, adding code produced relative gains of up to 8.2% in natural language reasoning, 4.2% in world knowledge, and 6.6% in generative win-rates, along with a 12x boost in code performance. (The addition of code results in those relative increases respectively.)
- The authors conclude that code is a critical building block for generalization far beyond coding tasks, and that improving code quality has an outsized effect across all tasks.
- Per a third-party review, gains were larger when high-quality synthetic code was included, which suggests dataset quality matters alongside quantity. I could not verify this in the primary paper text I found.
- Per the same review, a 50/50 code-to-text mix improved code generation but hurt natural language reasoning. I also could not confirm this from the paper itself, so treat it as secondhand.

**Takeaway:** The authors recommend investments in code quality and preserving code during pre-training, which they say have positive impacts.

For the full methodology and tables, the arXiv HTML version (arxiv.org/html/2408.10914v1) or the ICLR 2025 PDF are the primary sources.

Both papers are on arXiv, and both address how to choose the mix of training data for language models.

**RegMix (arXiv:2407.01492)**
- RegMix formulates the mixture choice as a regression task. It trains a set of small models on different data mixtures and fits a regression model to predict each mixture's performance.
- In the authors' experiments, the team trained 512 models with 1M parameters for 1B tokens and used the fitted model to pick the best mixture. That mixture was then used to train a 1B parameter model for 25B tokens, which performed best among 64 candidate 1B models with other mixtures.
- RegMix consistently outperformed human selection in experiments involving models up to 7B parameters trained on 100B tokens, while matching or exceeding DoReMi using just 10% of the computational resources.
- One finding is that web corpora rather than data perceived as high-quality like Wikipedia have the strongest positive correlation with downstream performance.
- It was published at ICLR 2025 (International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2025), and the authors released code at github.com/sail-sg/regmix.

**Scaling Laws for Optimal Data Mixtures (arXiv:2507.09404)**
- The paper is by Mustafa Shukor and colleagues at Sorbonne University and Apple. It proposes a systematic method to determine the optimal data mixture for any target domain using scaling laws.
- The approach predicts the loss of a model of size N trained with D tokens and a specific domain weight vector h.
- The authors tested this in three distinct and large-scale settings: large language model (LLM), native multimodal model (NMM), and large vision models (LVM) pretraining.
- Their parameters can be estimated using a few small-scale training runs, and the laws allow the derivation of optimal domain weights for any target domain under a given training budget.
- It was presented as a 2025 Poster at NeurIPS 2025.

**How they relate:** Both use small-scale runs to choose a data mixture before committing to a large training run. RegMix fits a regression on mixture-to-performance results, while the Apple/Sorbonne paper fits explicit scaling laws that model loss as a function of model size, token count, and domain weights.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

HP = dict(batch=64, lr=1e-3, wd=0.1, warmup_frac=0.03, final_lr_frac=0.1, betas=(0.9, 0.95), clip=1.0)

    a = np.load(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, f"{name}_{split}.npy"), mmap_mode="r")
    return torch.from_numpy(np.ascontiguousarray(a).astype(np.int16)).to(device)  # vocab < 32768

def val_loss(model, pool, ctx, max_tokens=1_000_000, bs=128):

    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True

               tokens_seen=dict(zip(DOMAINS, seen.tolist())), steps=steps, val_loss=vl, train_log=log,
               train_time_s=train_time, n_params=n_params(model), hp={**HP, **CONFIG})
    os.makedirs(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "pretrain"), exist_ok=True)
    json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "pretrain", args.name + ".json"), "w"), indent=1)
    if not args.no_save:
        os.makedirs(CKPT_DIR, exist_ok=True)

# Planning: Data Mixture Laws

*Written before any model was trained. Deviations are logged at the bottom.*

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters
The composition of a pre-training corpus (how much web text, code, encyclopedic text, papers…) is chosen
mostly by heuristics, yet it is one of the few levers that changes what a model can do at a fixed compute
budget. If downstream performance followed a simple, predictable law in the domain proportions, mixtures
could be chosen from a handful of small runs instead of trial and error at scale.

### Gap in Existing Work
- *Data Mixing Laws* (Ye et al., ICLR 2025) and *Scaling Laws for Optimal Data Mixtures* (Shukor et al.,
  NeurIPS 2025) fit functional forms to **validation loss**, not to downstream task accuracy.
- *RegMix* (Liu et al., ICLR 2025) regresses a loss target on mixtures and reports which domains correlate
  with downstream performance (web, not Wikipedia), but does not characterise the *shape* of the
  proportion→performance curve (log-linear? where does it saturate?).
- *To Code, or Not To Code?* (Aryabumi et al., ICLR 2025) shows code helps reasoning/knowledge tasks, but
  with a handful of mixtures, not a dose–response curve.
Nobody has (to our knowledge) jointly tested the specific shape claims in our hypothesis: log-linearity,
a ~20% saturation point, a code→reasoning correlation above 0.7, and a web>50% penalty on knowledge tasks.

### Our Novel Contribution
A controlled dose–response study: ~60 small GPTs trained from scratch at a fixed token budget on
systematically varied 4-domain mixtures, each evaluated on (a) per-domain held-out loss, (b) zero-shot
knowledge QA, and (c) fine-tuning transfer to reasoning tasks, with seed replicates to quantify noise and
pre-specified statistical tests for each of the hypothesis' four claims.

### Experiment Justification
- **E1 – single-domain sweeps** (each domain's share p ∈ {0,…,1}, others split the rest equally): the only
  way to see the *shape* of performance vs. proportion and to locate a saturation point (H1, H2, H4).
- **E2 – random simplex mixtures** (Dirichlet): an unbiased design for correlations and for fitting /
  cross-validating a mixture regression, so that domain effects are not confounded with the sweep
  structure (H3, and predictive "law" check).
- **E3 – seed replicates**: without a noise floor no curve-shape comparison or "degradation" claim is
  interpretable.
- **E4 – no-pre-training control** for the fine-tuned reasoning probes: establishes whether there is any
  transfer at all to measure.

## Research Question
At fixed model size and token budget, how does downstream performance depend on the proportion of each
domain in the pre-training mixture — is it log-linear with saturation near 20%, is code the strongest
driver of reasoning performance, and does >50% web text hurt knowledge-intensive tasks?

## Hypothesis Decomposition
- **H1 (log-linear):** along a single-domain sweep, performance is better described by `a + b·log(p)` than
  by `a + b·p`. Test: leave-one-out CV error and AICc of linear vs log-linear vs exponential
  (Ye et al. form) vs log-linear-with-plateau fits, for p > 0.
- **H2 (saturation at ~20%):** most of the gain from a domain is obtained by p = 0.2. Test: fraction of the
  total p=0→p=best improvement achieved at p=0.2; breakpoint of a fitted hinge model with bootstrap CI;
  whether performance beyond 0.2 differs from the 0.2 level by more than seed noise.
- **H3 (code → reasoning, r > 0.7):** across the random mixtures, Pearson/Spearman correlation between
  code share and the reasoning score exceeds 0.7 and exceeds that of every other domain. Also reported:
  mixture-regression (Scheffé) coefficients, since shares on a simplex are mutually negatively correlated.
- **H4 (web > 50% hurts knowledge):** in the web sweep, knowledge score at p ∈ {0.75, 1.0} is lower than at
  p ≤ 0.5 by more than seed noise (Welch t-test on seed replicates; monotone-trend test).

Independent variable: mixture vector over {web, wiki, code, arxiv}. Dependent variables below.
Controlled: architecture, tokenizer, token budget, optimiser, schedule, eval protocol.

## Proposed Methodology

### Approach
Training real language models from scratch is the only direct test; the price is scale
(34M-parameter GPT, 100M tokens/run). All conclusions are therefore about this small-scale regime and are
stated as such. No LLM APIs are needed.

- **Domains:** web = C4-en; wiki = WikiText-103; code = GitHub Python (codeparrot-clean);
  arxiv = scientific article bodies (ccdv/arxiv-summarization). Equal-size token pools; shared 16k BPE
  trained on a balanced sample.
- **Model:** 8-layer, 512-wide GPT, context 512; AdamW, cosine schedule, bf16 autocast.
- **Mixtures:** (E1) for each domain p ∈ {0, .02, .05, .1, .2, .35, .5, .75, 1}, remainder split equally;
  (E2) ~20 Dirichlet(1,1,1,1) draws; (E3) 3 seeds for the uniform mix and for the web-sweep points
  {.2, .5, .75, 1} (needed for H4), plus extra seeds on the code sweep if budget allows.

### Evaluation Metrics
1. **Per-domain held-out loss** (nats/token) — the quantity prior mixing laws model.
2. **Knowledge-intensive tasks, zero-shot multiple choice** scored by length-normalised answer
   log-likelihood: SciQ, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA. Tasks on which the *uniform*
   pilot model is not above chance are reported but excluded from the composite (decided on the pilot
   only, before any mixture comparison).
3. **Reasoning tasks, fixed-budget fine-tuning transfer** (tiny models cannot do zero-shot reasoning):
   ProofWriter (deductive, natural language), ListOps (hierarchical symbolic), multi-digit arithmetic.
   Accuracy after an identical, small fine-tuning budget. Control: randomly initialised model.
4. **Composites:** mean accuracy over tasks within a family (and z-scored mean as a robustness check).

### Baselines
Uniform mixture (0.25 each); single-domain models (p = 1); leave-one-domain-out models (p = 0);
no-pre-training control for reasoning probes; chance level for MC tasks. For curve shape: linear fit as
the null against log-linear.

### Statistical Analysis Plan
α = 0.05. Curve-shape: LOO-CV RMSE and AICc per (domain, metric). Correlations: Pearson and Spearman with
bootstrap 95% CIs over runs; Holm correction across the 4 domains. Degradation tests: Welch t-test across
seeds, effect size as difference in accuracy points with CI; item-level paired bootstrap as a secondary
check. Noise floor: SD across seeds for every metric.

## Expected Outcomes
Support: log fits beat linear fits on most (domain, metric) pairs; ≥ ~80% of gains realised by p = 0.2;
code share has the largest positive correlation with reasoning (> 0.7); knowledge score drops beyond 50%
web. Refutation: any of these failing beyond seed noise. Partial outcomes are reported per claim.

## Timeline
Data + tokenizer 20 min · pilot + eval harness 40 min · ~60 pre-training runs on 3–4 GPUs ≈ 2 h ·
evaluation ≈ 40 min · analysis 40 min · report 30 min.

## Potential Challenges
- Zero-shot knowledge accuracy near chance at this scale → composite restricted to tasks above chance;
  if none, fall back to fine-tuned closed-book QA and say so.
- Fine-tuning probes at floor/ceiling → calibrate budget on the uniform pilot + random-init control only.
- Shared GPUs / nearly full data disk → large artefacts on a scratch disk; scheduler skips busy GPUs.
- Simplex confound (raising one share lowers the others) → report regression coefficients, not only
  marginal correlations.

## Success Criteria
Each of H1–H4 receives a clear supported / not supported / inconclusive verdict backed by a test and a
noise estimate, with all runs, raw outputs and code saved.

"""Downstream task data.

Knowledge-intensive tasks (zero-shot multiple choice): SciQ, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA,
CommonsenseQA.  All official splits are pooled because nothing is trained on them.

Reasoning tasks (fixed-budget fine-tuning): ProofWriter (real data), ListOps and multi-digit
arithmetic (procedurally generated with fixed seeds, as in the original benchmarks).
"""
import random

import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download


def _pq(repo, fname):
    return pq.read_table(hf_hub_download(repo, fname, repo_type="dataset")).to_pandas()


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- knowledge (MC)
def _choices_fmt(df, qcol):
    items = []
    for r in df.itertuples():
        ch = getattr(r, "choices")
        labels, texts = list(ch["label"]), list(ch["text"])
        if r.answerKey not in labels:
            continue
        items.append((getattr(r, qcol), texts, labels.index(r.answerKey)))
    return items


def load_knowledge():
    """Returns {task: [(question, [choices], gold_index), ...]}."""
    rng = random.Random(0)
    out = {}
    sciq = []
    for sp in ["train", "validation", "test"]:
        for r in _pq("allenai/sciq", f"data/{sp}-00000-of-00001.parquet").itertuples():
            ch = [r.correct_answer, r.distractor1, r.distractor2, r.distractor3]
            order = list(range(4))
            rng.shuffle(order)
            sciq.append((r.question, [ch[i] for i in order], order.index(0)))
    out["sciq"] = sciq
    for cfg, key in [("ARC-Easy", "arc_easy"), ("ARC-Challenge", "arc_challenge")]:
        out[key] = sum((_choices_fmt(_pq("allenai/ai2_arc", f"{cfg}/{sp}-00000-of-00001.parquet"), "question")
                        for sp in ["train", "validation", "test"]), [])
    out["openbookqa"] = sum((_choices_fmt(_pq("allenai/openbookqa", f"main/{sp}-00000-of-00001.parquet"), "question_stem")
                             for sp in ["train", "validation", "test"]), [])
    # CommonsenseQA test labels are hidden -> train + validation
    out["commonsenseqa"] = sum((_choices_fmt(_pq("tau/commonsense_qa", f"data/{sp}-00000-of-00001.parquet"), "question")
                                for sp in ["train", "validation"]), [])
    return out


def mc_prompt(q):
    return f"Question: {q.strip()}\nAnswer:"


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- reasoning (fine-tune)
def proofwriter(n_train, n_test, max_chars=700, seed=0):
    """Deductive reasoning over natural-language rules; 3-way True / False / Unknown, class balanced.
    Only questions that need at least one inference step (QDep >= 1) or are Unknown are kept so
    that the task cannot be solved by string lookup alone."""
    def prep(df, n, rng):
        df = df[(df.theory.str.len() <= max_chars) & ~df.config.str.contains("NatLang")]
        df = df[(df.QDep >= 1) | (df.answer == "Unknown")]
        per = n // 3
        ex = []
        for a in ["True", "False", "Unknown"]:
            sub = df[df.answer == a]
            idx = rng.sample(range(len(sub)), per)
            ex += [(f"{r.theory}\nQuestion: {r.question}\nAnswer:", " " + r.answer) for r in sub.iloc[idx].itertuples()]
        rng.shuffle(ex)
        return ex
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    tr = _pq("tasksource/proofwriter", "data/train-00000-of-00002-6176cf3d78f48858.parquet")
    te = _pq("tasksource/proofwriter", "data/test-00000-of-00001-3e27b013c60e12d8.parquet")
    return prep(tr, n_train, rng), prep(te, n_test, rng)


def _listops_expr(rng, depth, max_args=4):
    if depth == 0 or rng.random() < 0.25:
        v = rng.randrange(10)
        return str(v), v
    op = rng.choice(["MAX", "MIN", "MED", "SM"])
    args = [_listops_expr(rng, depth - 1, max_args) for _ in range(rng.randint(2, max_args))]
    vals = [a[1] for a in args]
    v = {"MAX": max(vals), "MIN": min(vals), "MED": sorted(vals)[len(vals) // 2], "SM": sum(vals) % 10}[op]
    return "[ " + op + " " + " ".join(a[0] for a in args) + " ]", v


def listops(n_train, n_test, seed=0):
    """ListOps (Nangia & Bowman 2018): nested MAX/MIN/MED/SUM-mod-10 expressions, 10-way answer."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    seen, ex = set(), []
    while len(ex) < n_train + n_test:
        s, v = _listops_expr(rng, 3)
        if s.startswith("[") and s not in seen and len(s) < 160:
            seen.add(s)
            ex.append((s + " =", " " + str(v)))
    return ex[:n_train], ex[n_train:]


def arithmetic(n_train, n_test, seed=0):
    """3-digit addition / subtraction, digits space-separated; exact match on the full answer."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    seen, ex = set(), []
    while len(ex) < n_train + n_test:
        a, b, op = rng.randrange(100, 1000), rng.randrange(100, 1000), rng.choice("+-")
        if op == "-" and b > a:
            a, b = b, a
        if (a, b, op) in seen:
            continue
        seen.add((a, b, op))
        r = a + b if op == "+" else a - b
        sp = lambda n: " ".join(str(n))
        ex.append((f"{sp(a)} {op} {sp(b)} =", " " + sp(r)))
    return ex[:n_train], ex[n_train:]


# fixed fine-tuning budgets (calibrated once on the uniform-mixture pilot and a random-init control)
REASONING = {
    "proofwriter": dict(fn=proofwriter, n_train=3000, n_test=1500, steps=500, bs=32, lr=3e-4),
    "listops": dict(fn=listops, n_train=4000, n_test=2000, steps=500, bs=64, lr=3e-4),
    "arithmetic": dict(fn=arithmetic, n_train=4000, n_test=2000, steps=500, bs=64, lr=3e-4),
}

import json
import os
import time

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from tokenizers import Tokenizer

from model import build
from tasks import REASONING, load_knowledge, mc_prompt

        model.load_state_dict({k: v.float() for k, v in sd.items()})
    return model

    flat = []  # (item, choice, ids, n_prompt)

    order = sorted(range(len(flat)), key=lambda k: len(flat[k][2]))  # length-bucketed batches

        chunk = [flat[k] for k in order[b:b + bs]]
        x = pad_batch([c[2] for c in chunk])

"""Experiment design + a small GPU scheduler for a *shared* machine.

  python src/run_all.py --stage train    # pre-train every mixture in the design
  python src/run_all.py --stage eval     # downstream evaluation of every checkpoint
  python src/run_all.py --list           # print the design

The scheduler launches at most one of our jobs per GPU, and only on GPUs that currently have
MIN_FREE_MB of free memory (other users' jobs are never touched). Jobs that crash (e.g. OOM
because a neighbour grew) are re-queued. Finished jobs are skipped, so the script is resumable.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import numpy as np

from common import CKPT_DIR, DOMAINS, RESULTS_DIR, ROOT

SWEEP_P = [1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.75, 0.05, 0.1, 0.35, 0.02]   # priority order (coarse grid first)
N_RANDOM = 16
REPL_SEEDS = [1, 2]
WEB_REPL_P = [0.5, 1.0, 0.75, 0.2]
MIN_FREE_MB = 11000
MAX_TRIES = 4


def sweep_mix(dom, p):
    """Domain `dom` gets share p; the other three share the remainder equally."""
    m = np.full(len(DOMAINS), (1 - p) / (len(DOMAINS) - 1))
    m[DOMAINS.index(dom)] = p
    return m


def design():
    """Ordered list of runs: dict(name, mix, seed, group)."""
    runs = [dict(name="uniform_s0", mix=np.full(4, 0.25), seed=0, group="uniform")]
    for p in SWEEP_P:
        for d in DOMAINS:
            runs.append(dict(name=f"{d}_p{p:.2f}_s0", mix=sweep_mix(d, p), seed=0, group=f"sweep_{d}"))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
    rand = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(4), size=N_RANDOM)
    repl = [dict(name=f"uniform_s{s}", mix=np.full(4, 0.25), seed=s, group="uniform") for s in REPL_SEEDS]
    repl += [dict(name=f"web_p{p:.2f}_s{s}", mix=sweep_mix("web", p), seed=s, group="sweep_web")
             for p in WEB_REPL_P for s in REPL_SEEDS]
    rnd = [dict(name=f"rand{i:02d}_s0", mix=rand[i], seed=0, group="random") for i in range(N_RANDOM)]
    # interleave replicates and random mixtures so that a truncated run still covers both
    while repl or rnd:
        if rnd:
            runs.append(rnd.pop(0))
        if repl:
            runs.append(repl.pop(0))
        if rnd:
            runs.append(rnd.pop(0))
    return runs


def free_gpus(busy):
    out = subprocess.run(["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=index,memory.total,memory.used", "--format=csv,noheader,nounits"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    res = []
    for line in out.strip().splitlines():
        i, tot, used = [int(x) for x in line.split(",")]
        if i not in busy and tot - used >= MIN_FREE_MB:
            res.append((tot - used, i))
    return [i for _, i in sorted(res, reverse=True)]


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--stage", choices=["train", "eval"], default="train")
    ap.add_argument("--list", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=None, help="only the first N runs of the design")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    runs = design()[: args.limit]
    if args.list:
        for r in runs:
            print(r["name"], np.round(r["mix"], 3).tolist(), r["group"])
        print(len(runs), "runs")
        return
    json.dump([{**r, "mix": r["mix"].tolist()} for r in design()], open(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "design.json"), "w"), indent=1)
    py, src = sys.executable, os.path.join(ROOT, "src")
    queue = []
    for r in runs:
        if args.stage == "train":
            done = os.path.exists(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "pretrain", r["name"] + ".json"))
            cmd = [py, f"{src}/train.py", "--name", r["name"], "--mix", ",".join(f"{x:.6f}" for x in r["mix"]), "--seed", str(r["seed"])]
        else:
            path = os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "evals", r["name"] + ".json")
            done = os.path.exists(path) and "reason/arithmetic" in json.load(open(path))
            cmd = [py, f"{src}/evaluate.py", "--name", r["name"]]
            if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(CKPT_DIR, r["name"] + ".pt")):
                continue
        if not done:
            queue.append((r["name"], cmd, 0))
    print(f"{len(queue)} jobs queued", flush=True)
    log_dir = os.path.join(ROOT, "logs", "runs")
    os.makedirs(log_dir, exist_ok=True)
    running = {}  # gpu -> (name, cmd, tries, proc, t0)

  python src/run_all.py --stage train    # pre-train every mixture in the design

MIN_FREE_MB of free memory (other users' jobs are never touched). Jobs that crash (e.g. OOM
because a neighbour grew) are re-queued. Finished jobs are skipped, so the script is resumable.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import numpy as np

from common import CKPT_DIR, DOMAINS, RESULTS_DIR, ROOT

SWEEP_P = [1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.75, 0.05, 0.1, 0.35, 0.02]   # priority order (coarse grid first)
N_RANDOM = 16
REPL_SEEDS = [1, 2]
WEB_REPL_P = [0.5, 1.0, 0.75, 0.2]
MIN_FREE_MB = 11000
MAX_TRIES = 4


def sweep_mix(dom, p):
    """Domain `dom` gets share p; the other three share the remainder equally."""
    m = np.full(len(DOMAINS), (1 - p) / (len(DOMAINS) - 1))
    m[DOMAINS.index(dom)] = p
    return m


def design():
    """Ordered list of runs: dict(name, mix, seed, group)."""
    runs = [dict(name="uniform_s0", mix=np.full(4, 0.25), seed=0, group="uniform")]
    for p in SWEEP_P:
        for d in DOMAINS:
            runs.append(dict(name=f"{d}_p{p:.2f}_s0", mix=sweep_mix(d, p), seed=0, group=f"sweep_{d}"))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
    rand = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(4), size=N_RANDOM)
    repl = [dict(name=f"uniform_s{s}", mix=np.full(4, 0.25), seed=s, group="uniform") for s in REPL_SEEDS]
    repl += [dict(name=f"web_p{p:.2f}_s{s}", mix=sweep_mix("web", p), seed=s, group="sweep_web")
             for p in WEB_REPL_P for s in REPL_SEEDS]
    rnd = [dict(name=f"rand{i:02d}_s0", mix=rand[i], seed=0, group="random") for i in range(N_RANDOM)]

    while repl or rnd:
        if rnd:
            runs.append(rnd.pop(0))
        if repl:
            runs.append(repl.pop(0))
        if rnd:
            runs.append(rnd.pop(0))

    out = subprocess.run(["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=index,memory.total,memory.used", "--format=csv,noheader,nounits"],

            if rc != 0 and tries + 1 < MAX_TRIES:

"""Experiment design + a small GPU scheduler for a *shared* machine.

  python src/run_all.py --stage train    # pre-train every mixture in the design
  python src/run_all.py --stage eval     # downstream evaluation of every checkpoint
  python src/run_all.py --list           # print the design

The scheduler launches at most one of our jobs per GPU, and only on GPUs that currently have
MIN_FREE_MB of free memory (other users' jobs are never touched). Jobs that crash (e.g. OOM
because a neighbour grew) are re-queued. Finished jobs are skipped, so the script is resumable.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import numpy as np

from common import CKPT_DIR, DOMAINS, RESULTS_DIR, ROOT

SWEEP_P = [1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.75, 0.05, 0.1, 0.35, 0.02]   # priority order (coarse grid first)
N_RANDOM = 16
REPL_SEEDS = [1, 2]
WEB_REPL_P = [0.5, 1.0, 0.75, 0.2]
MIN_FREE_MB = 7000
MAX_TRIES = 4


def sweep_mix(dom, p):
    """Domain `dom` gets share p; the other three share the remainder equally."""
    m = np.full(len(DOMAINS), (1 - p) / (len(DOMAINS) - 1))
    m[DOMAINS.index(dom)] = p
    return m


def design():
    """Ordered list of runs: dict(name, mix, seed, group)."""
    runs = [dict(name="uniform_s0", mix=np.full(4, 0.25), seed=0, group="uniform")]
    for p in SWEEP_P:
        for d in DOMAINS:
            runs.append(dict(name=f"{d}_p{p:.2f}_s0", mix=sweep_mix(d, p), seed=0, group=f"sweep_{d}"))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
    rand = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(4), size=N_RANDOM)
    repl = [dict(name=f"uniform_s{s}", mix=np.full(4, 0.25), seed=s, group="uniform") for s in REPL_SEEDS]
    repl += [dict(name=f"web_p{p:.2f}_s{s}", mix=sweep_mix("web", p), seed=s, group="sweep_web")
             for p in WEB_REPL_P for s in REPL_SEEDS]
    rnd = [dict(name=f"rand{i:02d}_s0", mix=rand[i], seed=0, group="random") for i in range(N_RANDOM)]
    # interleave replicates and random mixtures so that a truncated run still covers both
    while repl or rnd:
        if rnd:
            runs.append(rnd.pop(0))
        if repl:
            runs.append(repl.pop(0))
        if rnd:
            runs.append(rnd.pop(0))
    return runs


def free_gpus(busy):
    out = subprocess.run(["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=index,memory.total,memory.used", "--format=csv,noheader,nounits"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    res = []
    for line in out.strip().splitlines():
        i, tot, used = [int(x) for x in line.split(",")]
        if i not in busy and tot - used >= MIN_FREE_MB:
            res.append((tot - used, i))
    return [i for _, i in sorted(res, reverse=True)]


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--stage", choices=["train", "eval"], default="train")
    ap.add_argument("--list", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=None, help="only the first N runs of the design")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    runs = design()[: args.limit]
    if args.list:
        for r in runs:
            print(r["name"], np.round(r["mix"], 3).tolist(), r["group"])
        print(len(runs), "runs")
        return
    json.dump([{**r, "mix": r["mix"].tolist()} for r in design()], open(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "design.json"), "w"), indent=1)
    py, src = sys.executable, os.path.join(ROOT, "src")
    queue = []
    for r in runs:
        if args.stage == "train":
            done = os.path.exists(os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "pretrain", r["name"] + ".json"))
            cmd = [py, f"{src}/train.py", "--name", r["name"], "--mix", ",".join(f"{x:.6f}" for x in r["mix"]), "--seed", str(r["seed"])]
        else:
            path = os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "evals", r["name"] + ".json")
            done = os.path.exists(path) and "reason/arithmetic" in json.load(open(path))
            cmd = [py, f"{src}/evaluate.py", "--name", r["name"]]
            if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(CKPT_DIR, r["name"] + ".pt")):
                continue
        if not done:
            queue.append((r["name"], cmd, 0))
    print(f"{len(queue)} jobs queued", flush=True)
    log_dir = os.path.join(ROOT, "logs", "runs")
    os.makedirs(log_dir, exist_ok=True)
    running = {}  # gpu -> (name, cmd, tries, proc, t0)
    env0 = {**os.environ, "CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER": "PCI_BUS_ID"}
    while queue or running:
        for gpu, (name, cmd, tries, proc, t0) in list(running.items()):
            rc = proc.poll()
            if rc is None:
                continue
            del running[gpu]
            print(f"[{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}] {name} on gpu{gpu} rc={rc} {time.time()-t0:.0f}s; {len(queue)} left", flush=True)
            if rc != 0 and tries + 1 < MAX_TRIES:
                queue.append((name, cmd, tries + 1))
        if queue:
            for gpu in free_gpus(running):
                if not queue:
                    break
                name, cmd, tries = queue.pop(0)
                f = open(os.path.join(log_dir, f"{args.stage}_{name}.log"), "a")
                proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=f, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, env={**env0, "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES": str(gpu)})
                running[gpu] = (name, cmd, tries, proc, time.time())
                time.sleep(20)  # let the job allocate before re-reading free memory
        time.sleep(10)
    print("ALL DONE", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Literature Review (compiled by the experiment runner)

The automated resource-finding stage was **skipped** for this workspace (`.neurico/pipeline_state.json`:
`"skipped": true`), so no papers, datasets or code were pre-gathered. This short review was assembled at
the start of the session. The first four entries were checked by web search (abstract-level only — the
PDFs were not downloaded or read in full); the last group is from the author's background knowledge and
was not re-verified.

## Verified (abstract level)

**Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance** — Ye, Liu, Sun,
Zhan, Zhou, Qiu. ICLR 2025, arXiv:2403.16952. Claims that model performance (validation loss) is a
predictable function of mixture proportions; fits functional forms ("data mixing laws", exponential in
the proportions) on a few sampled mixtures and nests them with step/size scaling laws to choose a
mixture for a 1B model on RedPajama. *Relevance:* closest prior work; its target is validation loss, not
downstream accuracy, and its functional form is exponential-in-proportion rather than log-linear.

**RegMix: Data Mixture as Regression for Language Model Pre-training** — Liu et al. ICLR 2025,
arXiv:2407.01492. Trains many tiny models (512 × 1M parameters, 1B tokens) on random mixtures, fits a
regression from mixture to a target loss and transfers the best mixture to larger models. Reports that
web corpora, rather than "high-quality" sources such as Wikipedia, correlate most positively with
downstream performance. *Relevance:* validates the small-proxy-model methodology used here, and its web
finding runs against our hypothesis' claim that heavy web text hurts.

**To Code, or Not To Code? Exploring Impact of Code in Pre-training** — Aryabumi et al. (Cohere).
ICLR 2025, arXiv:2408.10914. Ablations on 470M–2.8B models; adding code to pre-training gives relative
gains of up to 8.2% on natural-language reasoning and 4.2% on world knowledge versus text-only
pre-training. *Relevance:* the direct motivation for the "code → reasoning" claim; it uses a few
mixtures rather than a dose–response curve.

**Scaling Laws for Optimal Data Mixtures** — Shukor et al. (Sorbonne/Apple). NeurIPS 2025,
arXiv:2507.09404. Extends scaling laws to predict loss as a function of model size, token count and
domain weights, fitted on small runs. *Relevance:* again a loss-level law.

## Background (not re-verified in this session)
- DoReMi (Xie et al., 2023) and DoGE (Fan et al., 2023): learn domain weights with a proxy model.
- Chinchilla / Kaplan-style scaling laws: loss is a power law in data and parameters, which is why a
  logarithmic dependence on the amount of in-domain data is the natural prior for H1.
- BabyLM-style work: models trained on ≤100M words are evaluated mostly by likelihood-based and
  fine-tuning protocols because zero-shot benchmark accuracy is near chance at that scale. This is why
  our reasoning tasks are measured by fine-tuning transfer.

## Implications for the design
1. Small proxy models on many mixtures are the accepted methodology (RegMix, Data Mixing Laws).
2. Prior laws target loss; the open question is whether *downstream* metrics follow similar shapes.
3. Proportions live on a simplex: raising one share lowers the others, so marginal correlations must be
   complemented by mixture-regression coefficients.
4. Published evidence disagrees on web text (RegMix: most useful) vs. the hypothesis (harmful >50%).

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-25919/bundled-skills/2.1.293/980ee413d6140fb2b6b5c04619d65b46/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |
